statements.claim: Krishna rode out of Dwaraka under the pretext of a hunt, with Satyaki beside him, and left his charioteer Daruka behind with orders to wait, tending and grooming the horses, until he returned on that very car.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v1-4: Krishna went to the Raivataka mountain 'under the pretext of hunting', taking Satyaki on his car and telling Pradyumna 'Follow me'; to Daruka: 'take charge of my chariot and wait here tending and grooming the horses... I shall re-enter Dwarkā on this very car'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, Krishna's son by Rukmini, followed on a chariot of his own swift enough to course over hills; within the twinkle of an eye they crossed to Nandana, the pleasure park of the gods, where Krishna uprooted the Parijata tree and laid it on Garuda's back before the eyes of the celestial guardians.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v6-9: Pradyumna 'followed Krishna from behind on a separate car capable of coursing on hills'; 'within the twinkle of an eye the intelligent Hari arrived at... the Nandana forest'; hosts of celestial warriors present; Krishna 'uprooted the Pārijāta tree and placed it on the back of Garuda even before their eyes'.

statements.claim: The tree itself, embodied, approached Krishna in prayer, and Krishna consoled it, telling it not to fear.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v10-11: 'the Pārijāta, having embodied itself, approached (with prayer) Kesava and Garuda'; 'The tree Pārijāta was consoled by the high souled Kesava and was told—"Do thou not fear, O tree"'.

statements.claim: The keepers of the garden ran to Indra, who came out on Airavata with his son Jayanta following on a chariot; at the eastern gate Indra asked what was going on, Krishna saluted him with his head and said he was only taking the excellent tree away for a ceremonious observance; Indra replied that the tree could not be taken without challenging him to fight and bade Krishna hurl his mace Kaumodaki as the first blow.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v13-18: keepers informed Mahendra; Indra 'came out mounted on Airāvata being followed from behind by Jayanta on a car'; 'who had by that time reached the Eastern gate, Indra said... what is this going on'; Kesava: 'I am only taking away this excellent tree for a ceremonious observance of your sister-in-law'; Sakra: 'thou shouldst not take away this tree... without challenging me to fight... hurling the Koumodaki mace at me'.

statements.claim: Krishna pierced Airavata with arrows fierce as thunder while Indra pierced Garuda with heavenly shafts, each cutting off the other's arrows; the twang of Indra's bow and of the Sharanga (Sranga) made the inhabitants of heaven swoon.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v19-22: Krishna pierced 'the excellent elephant of the king of the celestials, with sharp arrows fierce like thunder itself'; Indra pierced Garuda 'with excellent arrows of heavenly make' and cut off Kesava's arrows, which Mādhava likewise severed; 'at the sound of Mahendra's bow and at the twang of the Sranga bow, the inhabitants of heaven swooned away'.

statements.claim: Jayanta tried to pull the Parijata tree from Garuda's back; Krishna, catching sight of him, called out to Pradyumna to prevent him, and instantly Pradyumna opposed him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v23-24: 'the highly powerful Jayanta tried to remove the Pārijāta tree from the back of Garuda'; Krishna told Pradyumna 'Prevent him', and 'instantly the highly powerful son of Rukshmini opposed him (firmly)'.

statements.claim: Jayanta, foremost of victorious persons, smiled from his chariot and pierced Pradyumna all over with sharp arrows; Pradyumna — the god of love (Cupid) reborn, lotus-eyed — answered with arrows that moved like serpents; a fierce combat raged, the two foremost wielders of weapons using every offensive and defensive weapon, while gods, sages, Siddhas and Charanas beheld it struck with wonder.
statements.evidence: HV 1.220 v25-29: Jayanta, 'that foremost of victorious persons, began to pierce with sharp arrows smilingly the son of Rukshmini on all parts of his body'; 'The lotus-eyed god Cupid... pierced the son of Indra, with arrows looking like snakes'; the two 'foremost of the wielders of weapons, used offensive and defensive weapons against each other'; 'The gods, the sages, the Siddhas and the Chārnas, all beheld that fierce combat being much struck with wonder'.

statements.claim: A weapon of heavenly make struck Pradyumna's chariot, and the whole car burned down to ashes before the eyes of heaven — yet the fire could not touch the son of Rukmini, who stood unharmed in the open sky where his chariot had been.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'The car of the illustrious Pradyumna was burnt down by that weapon but it could not... consume the son of Rukshmini'; full passage HV 1.220 v45-49 (same Gutenberg text): Jayanta 'struck him with a weapon of heavenly make' which 'fell upon the top of the car of the son of Rukshmini', the car burnt down, and Pradyumna 'extricated himself from the burning chariot' and 'stationed himself in the heaven with bow in hand'.

statements.claim: Above them the duel of the fathers went on, bowstring against bowstring, while heaven watched the two sons — the one who had lost his chariot and still had not fallen.
statements.evidence: The Krishna-Indra duel does continue through ch. 220-221 and v29/v61 record the onlookers' wonder at the sons' combat; 'heaven was no longer watching only Krishna and Indra' is closing narrative emphasis rather than a discrete sourceable fact.

notes: Faithful scene-by-scene to HV 1.220 (pack + Gutenberg source; pack passage cuts off at v32, remainder verified in the same cited text). 'Indra cutting down Garuda's feathers with heavenly shafts' condenses v20 (piercing Garuda with heavenly arrows); the feather-plucking belongs to the next chapter (221), a harmless conflation of the same duel. The story omits the 'sister-in-law' clause of Krishna's reason (abbreviation only).

statements.claim: Brahmadatta was a Vajasaneyi Brahmana of the city of Shatpura, on the sacred bank of the river Avarta, a disciple of Yajnavalka, well-read in the four Vedas and their six auxiliary sciences, initiated into a sacrifice lasting a full year.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v1-3: 'in the city of Shatpura on the sacred bank of the good river Avarta... a Vajasaneyi Brāhmana, by name Brahmadatta, a disciple of Yajnawalka, well-read in the four Vedas and six Angas... was initiated into a Yajna extending over a year'.

statements.claim: The great sages gathered around Brahmadatta — Vyasa and Yajnavalka, Sumantu, Jaimini, Devala and others — and the account's own narrator was among the guests at that year-long rite; Vasudeva came with Devaki beside him, for Brahmadatta was an old friend and preceptor of the house, and day after day Devaki gave the beggars whatever they asked, in proportion to her husband's wealth.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v4-5: 'were present Vyasa, Yajnawalka, Sumantu, Jaimini, Dhritimān, Jajali, Devala and other great and leading Munis... And I too had gone there'; Vasudeva with Devaki 'repaired there for protecting him, for he was a class friend and preceptor of Anakadundubhi'; 'the pious Devaki distributed amongst the beggars various articles they wanted proportionate to the wealth of the intelligent Vasudeva'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha and the other Daityas of Shatpura, proud of a boon they had once won, assembled at the sacrificial ground and delivered their terms: a share of the offerings, the right to drink Soma, Brahmadatta's daughters, and his finest jewels — threatening that the yajna would not be allowed if refused.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v6-12: 'the inhabitants of Shatpura, Nikumbha and other Daityas, proud of their boon, assembled there and said: "Give us our share in the Yajna. We will drink Soma and Brahmadatta must give us his daughters... He should also give us the most valuable jems... If he transgresses this order we will not allow him to celebrate this Yajna"'.

statements.claim: Brahmadatta refused them to their faces: no portion of the offerings was laid down for them in the Vedas, the daughters would be conferred on proper bridegrooms following the Vedas, the whole collection of his jewels was theirs if they came to terms, and if they used force, 'the son of Devaki is my supporter'.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v13-16, Brahmadatta's speech near-verbatim: 'no portion of sacrificial offerings has been laid down for you in the Vedas... The daughters whom I shall give away in marriage I shall confer upon proper bridegrooms following the same Vedas with me... If you however come to terms I may give you the entire collection of my jewels. If you show your force I will not give that even for Devaki's son is my supporter'.

statements.claim: The Danavas resorted to force: they scattered the articles of the sacrifice about the ground and carried away his daughters; Vasudeva, helpless, thought of Krishna and of Balabhadra and Gada, and the moment he was thought of Krishna knew everything and told Pradyumna to proceed and save the maidens by his illusive power, saying he himself would follow soon with the Yadava army.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v17-19: 'the wicked Dānavas of Shatpura, Nikumbha and others began to scatter the articles of Yajna and carry away his daughters. Beholding the sacrificial articles robbed by the Asuras Anakadundubhi thought of the great Krishna, Balabhadra and Gada. As soon as he was thought of Krishna came to know of every thing and said to Pradyumna: "Proceed, O my son, and save the maidens by virtue of your illusive powers... I myself too will soon go to Shatpura with the Yādava army"'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, intelligent, powerful and ever obedient to his father, was in Shatpura within a moment and by his illusive power took away the maidens — every one of them — creating counterfeit figures so like the originals that no eye could tell them apart and setting them before the Daityas, and telling Devaki 'Be not afraid'; the demons seized the illusory maidens and entered their city well satisfied, while the true daughters were far beyond their reach, and the sacrifice went on according to the proper rites.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v20-24: Pradyumna 'went to Shatpura within a moment and took away the maidens by virtue of his illusive power. Creating their figures by his illusive power the pious son of Rukshmini kept them before the Daityas and said to Devaki "Be not afraid"... the irrepressible Daityas carried away the illusory maidens and entered their city with satisfaction'; 'that great and glorious Yajna was being celebrated according to proper rites'. 'So like the originals that no eye could tell them apart' is a gloss of the illusion, uncontradicted.

statements.claim: The invited kings began to arrive and encamp with their hosts near Shatpura: Jarasandha and Shishupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarashtra, the rulers of the Malava and Tangana lands, Rukmi, Shalya, Shakuni and many another warrior king.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v24-28 lists 'Jarāsandha, Shisupala, Dantavakra, the Pandavas, the sons of Dhritarāshtra, the Mālava and Tangana kings, Rukshmi, Ahvriti, Neela, Nārmada, Vinda, Anuvinda, Avantya, Shalya, Shakuni and other heroic, noble and warrior kings encamped near Shatpura' — the story's 'many another warrior king' covers the remainder.

statements.claim: Narada watched the kings arrive and, reflecting that all the Kshatriyas and Yadavas assembled at the yajna would surely lead to a conflict which he would try to bring about, went to the house of Nikumbha.
statements.evidence: HV 1.230 v29-30: 'the beautiful Nārada thought: "At this Yajna all the Kshatryas and Yādavas have assembled. Surely this will lead to a conflict. I shall therefore try to bring it about." Thinking this he repaired to Nikumbha's house'.

notes: Near-verbatim paraphrase of HV 1.230. 'The demons did not believe him' is the story's connective gloss for the demons' resort to force after the refusal. Vasudeva's helplessness and the general compression (kings listed via 'many another warrior king') are consistent with the pack.

statements.claim: By the middle of that day a cave near Shatpura had swallowed 'half the Yadava army'.
statements.evidence: Dramatic teaser of the capture scene the story then narrates in detail; the pack (HV 1.231 v27-29) supports Nikumbha carrying off Anadhristhi, Kritavarma, Charudeshna, Vaitarana, Sanatkumar, Arksha, Nishatha, Ulmuka 'and numerous other Yādavas' into the cave — not a quantified 'half'. Hyperbolic framing, no distortion of the record.

statements.claim: The kings who had come to witness Brahmadatta's sacrifice had stayed and, Narada's whispers having done their work, arrayed themselves with the Asuras against the Yadavas at dawn.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v17-22: 'the soldiers of the Chedi and other kings were bent upon assisting the Asuras'; Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni, Jarāsandha, Trigarta, Virāta, Uttara etc. 'got themselves ready' to fight the Yadavas; Narada's instigation is the closing beat of the previous event (HV 1.230 v29-30, corpus chain).

statements.claim: At dawn Baladeva, Krishna and Satyaki mounted Garuda, bathed in the sacred river Avarta — made holy by a boon of Rudra — put on coats of mail and finger-guards, and worshipped Shiva, the lord of the bel leaf and the waters; Pradyumna was placed in front of the army, the Pandavas in charge of the sacrifice, and soldiers at the door of the cave; Jayanta and Pravara arrived the instant Krishna thought of them and were posted above with Pradyumna.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v1-6: 'Within a moment of the clear sun coming... Baladeva, Krishna and Satyaki delightedly got upon Garuda's back. Having bathed in the water of the sacred river Avarta, who had obtained a boon from Rudra... and having put on coats of mail, finger-protectors and armours... worshipped the god Siva, the lord of bel leaves and water'; 'having placed Pradyumna above in front of the army, the Pandavas in charge of the Yajna and the remaining soldiers at the door of the cave'; Krishna thought of Jayanta and Pravara, who arrived at once 'and were kept above along with Pradyumna'.

statements.claim: The war-instruments sounded — conches, drums and battle-bugles; Samba and Gada drew up the soldiers in the shape of a makara; Uddhava, Kritavarma, Charudeshna, Sanatkumar and the rest guarded Aniruddha and protected the rear.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v7-10: 'at Krishna's mandate, war-bugles, Jalaja, Muraja and other musical instruments were sounded'; 'Sāmva and Gada arranged the soldiers in the shape of a Makara'; Shārana, Uddhava, Vaitarana, Anādhrishti, Viprithu, Prithu, Kritavarmā, Sudangsthra, Vichakshu, Sanatkumar and Chārudeshna 'began to help Aniruddha and protect the rear of the army'.

statements.claim: Out of Shatpura came the Danavas, dreadful in battle, roaring like gathering clouds — riding on asses and elephants, crocodiles and hares, horses, buffaloes, lions and tortoises, their chariots drawn by such beasts; Nikumbha came at their head as the lord of gods issues out at the head of the celestial host, and the earth and sky were filled with his shouts and leonine roars.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v11-16: the Dānavas 'came out of Shatpura, emitting a roar like the muttering of clouds, on asses, elephants, crocodiles, hares, horses, buffaloes, lions and tortoises. Many of their cars were drawn by those animals'; 'as the lord of gods issues out at the head of the celestial host so Nikumbha came out at the head of that Asura army'; 'sending up again and again shouts of various sorts and leonine roars the highly powerful Dānavas filled the earth and sky with them'.

statements.claim: Behind them came the kings: the hundred brothers of the Chedi king Shishupala, led by Duryodhana, wheeled and rattled with their chariots like the city of the Gandharvas; Rukmi and Ahvati joined them; Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni, Jarasandha, Trigarta, Virata and Uttara made ready for the encounter.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v17-22: 'amongst the followers of the Chedi king Shishupāla, the hundred brothers headed by Duryodhana stood there with their cars, making a great rattle and coursing quickly like unto the city of Gandharva'; 'Rukshmi and Ahvati joined them'; 'the king Bhagadatta, Shalya, Shakuni, Jarāsandha, Trigarta, Virāta, Uttara... got themselves ready for the encounter'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha struck first, pouring arrows like serpents into the Yadava ranks; Anadhristhi, commander-in-chief of the Yadu army, answered with arrows adorned with variegated feathers and whetted on stone until Nikumbha's chariot, standard and horses disappeared under the hail; Nikumbha then bewildered Anadhristhi by illusion, carried him off to the cave named Shatpura and imprisoned him there, and — invisible to every eye — returned to take Kritavarma, Charudeshna, Vaitarana of the Bhoja race, Sanatkumar, Arksha the son of Jambavati, Nishatha, Ulmuka and numerous other Yadavas, dragging them all into that dreadful cave.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v23-30: Nikumbha 'began to assail the dreadful army of the Bhaimas with arrows like serpents'; Anādhrishti, 'the commander-in-chief of the Yadu army', 'with shafts, adorned with variegated feathers and whetted on stone, began to slay the enemy's army'; 'Nikumbha, his chariot, standard and horses became invisible'; 'bewildering Anadhristhi and bringing him to the cave named Shatpura the heroic Nikumbha imprisoned him there'; returning, 'he, by his illusive powers, took there Kritavarmā, Chārudeshna, Vaitarana of Bhoja's race, Sanatkumār, Jāmvavati's son Arksha, Nishatha, Ulmuku and numerous other Yādavas', 'so covered himself by his illusive powers that no body could see him'.

statements.claim: Krishna set his Sharanga bow and moved among the Danavas as the god of fire ranges over dry grass; the demons hurled iron missiles and iron clubs, fiery lances and burning axes, great rocks and boulders, and whole elephants, chariots and horses; the Narayana fire consumed them all, and Krishna, smiling, baffled the demons with the fire of his arrows, bearing their onslaught as a bull bears the autumn rain.
statements.evidence: HV 1.231 v30-33: Krishna 'setting string to his Srānga bow and shooting arrows... began to move about amongst the Dānavas as the god of fire ranges on grass'; Danavas 'taking up thousands of Sataghnis, Parighas, fiery lances, burning axes, dreadful rocks, and huge stones and throwing up infuriated elephants, cars and horses'; 'Narayana-fire consumed all those things. And smiling the highly effulgent Yadu chief... baffled them all with the fire of his arrows. And as a bull suffers the downpour of rain in the autumn so he bore the shower'.

statements.claim: At Nandi's command, bearing the nooses given by Hara — by Shiva himself — Pradyumna moved among the kings who had sided with the Asuras, bound Bhagadatta, Shishupala, Rukmi, Ahvati and the other kings with those divine nooses, and took them all to the illusory cave.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'binding the king Bhagadatta, Shishupāla, Ahvati, Rukshmi and other kings... with the nooses given by Hara Rukshmini's son... took them all to the illusory cave'; full passage HV 1.231 v55-60 (same Gutenberg text): Nandi came 'taking up a thousand of nooses' and said 'Vilwodakeshwara (Siva) has ordered you to do what he had told you in the night. Bind these kings with nooses who have been bribed with jewels for the maidens', whereupon Pradyumna bound them 'like hissing serpents, with the nooses given by Hara' and 'took them all to the illusory cave'.

notes: Faithful to HV 1.231; the cave/'Shatpura' usage follows the pack (the Dutt text calls both the cave and the Danava abode 'Shatpura'). The closing image (the cave that swallowed the Yadava captains now holding the bribed kings, with Aniruddha posted as its guard) matches the passage. The 'half the army' teaser is hyperbole over a supported mass capture (see connective statement).

statements.claim: While the Yadavas were busy with their sports, Nikumbha, the master of illusion, slipped past the garden attached to the women's apartments — unapproachable but unguarded at that hour — and carried off Bhanumati, the beautiful daughter of Bhanu, remembering how Pradyumna had once carried away Prabhavati, daughter of his own brother Vajranabha, and had killed the brother besides.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v1-5: Nikumbha 'stole away the beautiful daughter of Bhānu by name Bhānumati'; 'formerly, the daughter of his brother Vajranābhā, by name Prabhāvati, had been taken away by Pradyumna and Vajranābha had been killed. Remembering this former enmity... he played upon the women of the Yādavas'; 'Although the garden, attached to the female appartment of Bhānu, was unapproachable, still at that time there were no guards for the Yadavas were busy with their sports'.

statements.claim: While the weeping maiden was being carried away a great tumult rose through the women's apartments and Vasudeva and Ahuka came out in a fury; Krishna, hearing of the insult, mounted Garuda with Arjuna beside him, commanded Pradyumna — whose banner bore the makara — to follow on his chariot, and they overtook the demon before he could reach the city of Vajra.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v6-11: 'while that weeping maiden was being carried away there arose all on a sudden a great tumult in the female appartment'; 'Vasudeva and Ahuka issued out, filled with wrath'; hearing of the insult Krishna 'rode, together with Pārtha, Garuda the enemy of the serpents'; 'having commanded the hero having the emblem of a Makara on his flag to follow him on his car'; 'before Nikumbha... could reach the city of Vajra, Pārtha and Krishna... overtook him in the way'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, foremost of those skilled in illusion, divided himself into three; Nikumbha, like an immortal, fought all three at once with heavy clubs — holding Bhanumati in his left hand and hurling the club with his right.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v12-14: Pradyumna 'divided himself into three portions'; 'Nikumbha, like unto an immortal, smilingly fought with them all with heavy clubs. Holding the maiden Bhānumati by his left hand, the great Asura Nikumbha repeatedly hurled the club with his right hand'.

statements.claim: Although any one of the three was capable of slaying the demon, none could strike him ruthlessly for fear of wounding the maiden in his arms; they fought with restraint, sighing piteously out of compassion for her, until Arjuna — as a man skilled in arms strikes the serpent coiled around a camel, leaving the camel unhurt — began to wound the demon with his cane-like arrows.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v15-18: 'none could strike him ruthlessly lest they might wound the maiden'; 'although capable of slaying that irrepressible enemy they began to sigh piteously out of their excessive compassion for the maiden'; 'As when a serpent gets round a camel, a man, well up in the use of arms, strikes the serpent leaving the camel to itself, so Pārtha, the foremost of archers, began to strike the Daitya with his arrows'; all three 'wounded the Danavas with their cane-like arrows'.

statements.claim: Nikumbha resorted to illusion and vanished with the maiden so completely that no one could tell where he had gone, and the three pursued him as he fled — now in the semblance of a yellow vulture — across the whole earth, over the seven insular continents, until he dropped down with the maiden on the bank of the river Chela Ganga, high on the summit of Mount Gokarna, a mountain none of the gods, Asuras or great ascetics could cross, protected by the energy of Mahadeva.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v19-24: 'resorting to his illusory powers Nikumbha so disappeared with the maiden from that place that nobody could know it: Krishna, Kāma and Dhananjaya however immediately pursued him: he, however, went on assuming the semblance of a yellow vulture'; 'travelled all over the earth consisting of seven insular continents and dropped down with the maiden at last on the bank of the river Chela Gangā flowing on the summit of the mount Gokarna'; 'None amongst the gods, Asuras or great ascetics could cross that mountain protected by the energy of Mahadeva'.

statements.claim: There Pradyumna seized Bhanumati from the demon, while Krishna and Arjuna drove Nikumbha from the northern range of Gokarna to the southern with their arrows, pursuing him on Garuda.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v25-26: 'the Bhaima chief Pradyumna... got hold of the maiden Bhānumati. And Krishna, and Arjuna began to assail the Asura greatly with arrows. Then leaving the northern range of the mount Gokarna, Nikumbha fled to the southern range. Both the Krishnas however, riding on Garuda, pursued him'.

statements.claim: Broken and furious, Nikumbha fled into Shatpura, the abode of his kinsmen; the two heroes spent the night at the mouth of the cave; with Krishna's permission Pradyumna carried Bhanumati back to Dwaraka in triumph, then returned to find Krishna and Arjuna waiting where he had left them, before the cave.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v27-29: 'the great Asura entered into Shatpura, the abode of his kinsmen and those two heroes spent the night at the mouth of the cave. With Krishna's permission the heroic son of Rukshmini delightedly took Bhaima's daughter to the city of Dwārakā. And keeping her there he returned to Shatpura... and beheld the two Krishnas of dreadful prowess at the mouth of the cave'.

statements.claim: Desirous of fighting, Nikumbha came out of the cave; Arjuna met him at the threshold with arrows from the Gandiva, blocking the way; it made no difference — Nikumbha came on, took up his club, a great staff covered with thorns, and struck Partha on the head, and Arjuna vomited blood and lost consciousness on the spot.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v31-34: 'desirous of fighting the highly powerful Nikumbha came out of the cave... Dhananjaya, with arrows shot off his Gandiva bow, obstructed the thorough-fair. In spite of it Nikumbha... came out, took up his club covered with thorns and struck Pārtha on his head. Thus assailed... Pritha's son vomitted blood and lost his consciousness'.

statements.claim: The master of illusions smiled and, with an unseen stroke of the same club, struck the heroic son of Rukmini — the foremost of those skilled in illusion — on the head, and Pradyumna fell senseless beside his friend; then Govinda, the king of Dwaraka, seized his club Kaumodaki and ran toward Nikumbha.
statements.evidence: HV 1.237 v34-35 and pack excerpt: 'The Asura, master of illusions, smilingly struck the heroic son of Rukshmini, the foremost of those conversant with illusions... Wounded on the head with that unseen stroke of the club the heroic Pradyumna lost his consciousness'; excerpt: 'Govinda... took up his club Koumodaki and ran towards Nikumbha'.

notes: Chapter title of HV 1.237 is itself 'Nikumbha Carries Away Bhanumati'; the story opens with the aftermath (the cave duel) then backtracks to the abduction — every scene maps to the pack's verses. Pack passage truncated mid-sentence at v34; the finale is confirmed by the pack's excerpt line.

statements.claim: The city of Vajra belonged to the Asura king Vajranabha, who had practised long austerities on the summit of Mount Sumeru until Brahma himself appeared and offered him a boon; Vajranabha asked for two things: that no god should ever be able to kill him, and that he should possess the city of Vajra — a city where even the air could not easily enter, ringed with gardens, with many branch cities, rich in peerless jewels, granting every wish before the wish was even spoken — and Brahma granted both.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v5-9: Vajranābha 'practised hard austerities on the summit of the mount Sumeru'; 'the Divine Brahmā... asked him to pray for a boon'; he 'prayed for two boons that even the gods might not kill him, and that he might get the city Vajra where even the air cannot easily enter, which gives every sort of desired-for objects even when they are not thought of, which has gardens encircled by walls, many branch cities, and peerless jems of every description'.

statements.claim: Millions of Asuras, enemies of the gods, took refuge with Vajranabha and lived in Vajra's gardens and branch cities, healthy, well-fed and content, safe under the shelter of the boon.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v11-12: 'seeking refuge with that great Asura who had obtained this boon, millions of demons lived in that city of Vajra, in his garden and in many charming branch cities... the enemies of the gods lived there, healthy, well-fed and contented'.

statements.claim: Elated by his good fortune, Vajranabha went to Indra and announced that the three worlds were the common property of all the high-souled sons of Kashyapa alike — he wished to govern them, and if Indra did not approve he could give battle; Indra consulted Brihaspati, and the two chose to wait, since their father Kashyapa was in the middle of a great sacrifice and would do what was fair when it ended; Vajranabha carried the same answer to Kashyapa himself, who sent him home with the same promise.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v13-19: Vajranābha told Indra 'all the three worlds are the common properties of all the high-souled sons of Kashyapa. I therefore wish to govern the three worlds. If you... do not approve of my proposal, give me battle'; Mahendra 'consulted with Vrihaspati', answering 'our father, the ascetic Kashyapa, is now engaged in a sacrifice. After its termination he will do what is fair'; Kashyapa told Vajranabha the same and sent him back to the city of Vajra.

statements.claim: Indra came secretly to Dwaraka and told Krishna everything; Krishna answered that the horse-sacrifice of Vasudeva, his father, was at hand and that once it was over he would kill Vajranabha, adding honestly that even the wind could not enter the city if Vajranabha did not wish it, and that they would find a way in at the right hour.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v20-23: 'Mahendra went to the city of Dwāravati... and communicated secretly to Vāsudeva what Vajranābha had said'; Janārddana: 'O Vāsava, the horse-sacrifice of Vasudeva is now at hand. After its termination I will kill Vajranabha... even the wind cannot enter into his city if Vajranābha does not wish it. At a convenient hour we will concert measures for entering there'.

statements.claim: During the horse-sacrifice itself, an actor named Bhadra so delighted the great saints that they invited him to ask for a boon; prompted by Krishna and as if urged on by the goddess of learning, he asked to roam freely over the seven continents of the earth and through the sky with nothing to obstruct him, to be strong and unharmed by any creature moving or still, to take whatever form he pleased, that age might never touch him, and that the sages might always be pleased with him — and the Munis said 'So be it'.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v26-32: Bhadra 'pleased the great saints with his beautiful acting. The leading Munis then asked him to pray for a boon'; he prayed 'as desired by Krishna and as if urged on by the goddess of learning': 'may I range over the earth consisting of seven insular continents... without any obstruction, range all over the sky... be gifted with strength and be not slain by all creatures mobile and immobile. May I assume any form I like... May not decrepitude overtake me and may the Munis always remain pleased with me'; 'the Munis said "So be it"'. (The story omits the first request — to become the food of all twice-born — an omission, not an error.)

statements.claim: From that day the immortal-looking actor ranged over the whole earth, performing in the cities of the Danava kings, in Uttarakuru, Bhadrashva, Ketumala and the island of Kalamra, and on every festival day he came back to Dwaraka, where the Yadavas welcomed him.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v33-35: 'That immortal-like one began to range all over the earth... He began to show his performances in the cities of the Dānava kings, in Uttarakura, Bhadrāshwa, Ketumāl and the island of Kalāmra. On the occasion of every Parva, that great actor... used to come to Dwarakā adorned with the Yadavas'.

statements.claim: Indra called the Dhartarashtra swans — celestial birds and his own brothers, since both gods and swans are begotten by Kashyapa — and told them the great duty of killing the enemies of the gods awaited them; they were to keep the counsel secret, go to the city of Vajra, where no one else could enter, and range in the tanks of the king's inner palace; there Vajranabha's daughter Prabhavati — fair as moonlight, the jewel of the three worlds, kept by her friends for a swayamvara — was to be won by hearing of the family, beauty, character and accomplishments of the high-souled Pradyumna; they were to carry her words to Pradyumna and bring back his, reporting to Indra and to his younger brother Krishna at Dwaraka every day.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v36-50 (pack excerpt + Gutenberg source; pack passage cut at v37): Sakra to the Dhārtarāshtra swans: 'you are our brothers on account of your being begotten by Kashyapa... don't divulge the counsel'; 'going to the most excellent city of Vajranabha where no one else can enter you should range in the tanks of his inner appartment'; 'Vajranābha has a jewel of a daughter, peerless in beauty, in the three worlds, by name Prabhāvati who is fair like the rays of the moon... her friends have kept that beautiful and chaste maiden for Swayemvara'; 'Do you describe to her the various accomplishments, family, beauty, character, and age, of the high-souled Pradyumna'; 'take carefully her news to Pradyumna and return with his message to her'; 'you should communicate to me and to my younger brother Krishna at Dwāravati daily what happens there'.

statements.claim: Indra told the swans that the Danavas — elated by the pride of Brahma's boon — could not be slain by the gods; their destruction had to come from the sons of the gods, from Pradyumna and his brothers; and since the actor Bhadra had obtained the boon of entering the city, the Yadavas would enter Vajra in his guise.
statements.evidence: HV 1.238 v51-52 (pack excerpt + Gutenberg source): 'Those Dānavas, elated with the pride of the boon conferred by Brahmā, are not to be slain by the gods. So their destruction in the battle-field should be brought about by Pradyumna and other sons of gods. An actor, Bhadra by name, has of late obtained the boon (of entering into his city). So the Yadavas, headed by Pradyumna, will enter into Vajranābha's city in his guise'.

statements.claim: So the swans rose into the sky and turned toward a city no army could approach, carrying a message that would open it from within — through the heart of the king's own daughter.
statements.evidence: Closing frame condensing the mission (chapter 239 opens with the celestial swans going to the city of Vajra); 'no army could approach' restates v40's 'where no one else can enter', and the courtship of Prabhavati is the mission per v43-47.

notes: Every element of the story — including Indra's full speech to the swans — matches HV 1.238 v36-54. The pack's own passage cuts off mid-speech at v37 ('[...]'); the remainder was verified in the same cited Gutenberg translation (chapter CCXXXVIII), and the pack's excerpt line independently confirms the speech's gist. The opening 'beyond the seven continents' is atmospheric color (the city's kingdom is later placed by Mount Sumeru, ch. 244).

statements.claim: Vajranabha's orders went ahead of the troupe: the Asuras of his cities were to give the actors the finest rooms, treat them as guests, and press jewels and fine raiment upon them; the actor who had won the sages' boon reached the dependent city of Supura and so delighted its citizens with his dancing that they welcomed him with presents.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v1-5: king Vajranābha ordered the Asuras of their cities: 'Give them most excellent rooms... Treat them as guests, give them various jewels and various raiments which please people'; 'Receiving the order of their Chief they did all this... With great delight they welcomed the actor with presents of jewels... the actor, who had obtained the boon, pleased highly the citizens of Supura with his dancing'.

statements.claim: The company staged the Ramayana — the birth of Vishnu for the destruction of Ravana, and how the kings Lomapada and Dasharatha brought the young sage Rishyashringa to Shanta — personating Rama, Lakshmana, Shatrughna and Bharata so perfectly that even the oldest Danavas were startled and spoke again and again of the resemblance; the delighted Danavas rose from their seats, applauded, and threw down necklaces of gold and vaidurya, bracelets and cloths, and the actors praised each Asura house in verse, in the order of its family and birth.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v6-13: 'They gave a performance of the great epic Rāmāyana: the birth of the incomparable Vishnu for the destruction of the king of Rakshasas (Ravana). How Lomapāda and Dasharatha had brought for Shānta, the Muni Rishwashringa'; 'the actors so perfectly personated the characters of Rāma, Lakshmana, Shatrughna, Bharata... that even the elderly Dānavas were startled and spoke repeatedly of the similarity'; the Asuras 'repeatedly rose up, expressed their appreciation and gave away charming necklaces of gold and Vaidurja, bracelets and cloths'; 'the actors, with separate slokas, eulogised the Asuras in order of their family and birth'.

statements.claim: The news reached the city of Vajra; Vajranabha, who had heard of the famous actor long before, sent a messenger, and the Daityas of the branch cities conducted the disguised Yadavas into the great city itself, lodging them in a beautiful house built by the celestial architect; Vajranabha raised a great pavilion, made a festival of the players, gave them profuse jewels after they had rested, and — keeping the women of his family behind a screen — sat with his kinsmen to watch the play.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v14-20: 'the inhabitants of the dependant cities communicated to Vajra nābha the arrival of the beautiful actors... pleased he sent a messenger to bring the actor'; 'the Daityas, living in branch cities, took the Yadavas, disguised as actors, to the charming city of Vajra'; 'a beautiful house, built by the celestial architect, was offered'; 'having set up a beautiful pandal the great Asura, Vajranābha, made a great festival with the actors. After they had been relieved of toil... Vajranābha gave profuse jems and requested them to begin the play'; 'having kept the women of his family behind a screen... the great Asura himself sat with his kinsmen'.

statements.claim: Dressed as actors, the young men of the Yadava house began the performance: first the music of kamsya, venu and muraja; then the women of the troupe sang the Gandharva song Chhalikya, sweet to ear and mind; and with the seven scales, the three gramas and the ragas of spring they sang the song of the sacred descent of the Ganga, so that the Asuras rose again and again in pleasure.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v21-25: 'dressing themselves as actors, and arranging for the concert the Bhaimas... went on with the performance. They first played various tunes on musical instruments, as Kansya, Venu, Muraja etc. Afterwards the women... sang the Gandharva song Chhalikya, delightful to the mind and ears. Then with seven scales, Gāndhāra and others, three Grāmas, and with Rāgas, Vasanta and others, they sang sweetly the song of the sacred discension of Ganga... Asuras rose up again and again and pleased the actors'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna, Gada and Shamba — all in the guise of actors — conducted the nandi, the opening benediction, and Rukmini's son sang the hymn of the Ganga's descent with graceful gestures; then came the drama Rambhabhisara, in which Shura played Ravana, Monovati played Rambha, Pradyumna played Nalakuvara and Shamba played the jester, the Yadavas by their illusory powers conjuring the very scene of Kailasa, where the angry Nalakuvara cursed Ravana and comforted Rambha.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v26-30: 'the powerful Pradyumna, who had assumed the guise of an actor, Gada and Shāmva conducted the Nāndi. After the termination of the Prologue Rukshmini's son sang the hymn, accompanied with beautiful gestures, of the descension of Gangā. Afterwards they began the performance of the drama Rambhābhisara, Shura acted the part of Rāvana, Monovati represented Rambhā, Pradyumna Nalakuvara and Shāmva his Vidushaka. By their illusory powers the Yādavas represented the scene of Kailāsha... how the wicked Rāvana was imprecated by Nalakuvara, worked up with anger and how Rambhā was consoled'.

statements.claim: Scene by scene the delighted Danavas showered the stage with costly garments, jewelled necklaces, sky-cars, celestial elephants, cool sandal and aloe scents, and at last the Chintamani, the gem that grants every wish — giving so freely at every scene that they drained their own treasuries, the women of the Asura chiefs among them.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v31-37: 'They gave them costly apparels, jewelleries, necklaces set with costly jems, beautiful balloons, cars ranging in the sky, elephants coursing in the etherial region, cool and celestial sandal, Agura, and other scents and the valuable jem Chintāmani which gives all that is thought of. Giving away presents in this way at every scene those Dānavas were deprived of their riches and jewels. Even the women of the Danava-Chiefs shared the same fate'.

statements.claim: Prabhavati's friend Suchimukhi, the goose, came to the princess and said she had gone secretly to Dwaraka, seen Pradyumna there, and told him of her love; he was pleased and had appointed this evening for meeting her — 'the Yadavas never speak an untruth. Truly, today you will meet your love'; Prabhavati's heart leapt, and she asked the goose to stay in her room that night, saying that with her beside her she feared nobody and wished to see Krishna's son.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v38-44: Suchimukhi: 'I had gone to the charming city of Dwārakā... I saw Pradyumna there secretly and told him about your love for him... Pleased he has appointed this evening for meeting you... the Bhaimas never speak an untruth; verily to-day you will meet your love'; Prabhāvati: 'to-day wait in my room and sleep here. If you live by me I do not fear any body. With you I wish to see Keshava's son'.

statements.claim: That evening a fragrant garland, thick with bees, was carried to the princess's chamber and set down near Prabhavati; hidden among the bees was Pradyumna, who had taken the form of one of them; as dusk turned to evening the other bees flew away one by one, and the one that remained, the hero of the Yadava house, slowly settled on Prabhavati's ear.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v49-53 + pack excerpt: 'seeing a fragrant garland filled with bees carried for Prabhāvati, the highly powerful... hero, Pradyumna... sat there on assuming the form of a bee. That garland, covered with black-bees, was taken by the maid servants to the inner appartment and kept near Prabhāvati... when gradually evening set in, the other bees fled away. Then having none to follow him the heroic Bhaima chief slowly sat on Prabhāvati's ear'.

statements.claim: The full moon rose, and Prabhavati, whose limbs burned and whose mouth had gone dry, confessed to the goose the strange fever of loving a man she had only heard of — 'I have not seen him, and still my limbs burn' — and then the bee at her ear was no bee at all: the guest promised for the evening had come, and that night the long-pining lovers met.
statements.evidence: HV 1.240 v54-62: 'beholding the highly charming full moon arise... Prabhāvati... said to the goose, "O friend, my limbs are burning, my mouth is being dried up... I have not seen him—I have wanted him after only hearing of him—still my limbs are burning"'; the meeting follows in HV 1.241 v1-3 (same source): Pradyumna tells the goose 'in the guise of a black-bee, I have come here... Let her do what she likes to do with me', and appears in his own form — consistent with the corpus-chain next beat and the pack's stated scope ('the long-pining lovers meet by night').

notes: Very faithful to HV 1.240, verse by verse through the whole festival and courtship. The pack's passage cuts off at v43 ('[...]'); the remainder (v44-62, bee scene) is confirmed verbatim in the same cited Gutenberg translation and by the pack's excerpt line. The closing 'lovers met at last' stops short of the marriage in ch. 241 — within scope, no error.

statements.claim: When the great sacrifice of the sage Kashyapa ended, gods and Asuras went back to their own habitations, and Vajranabha — still set on conquering the three worlds — went to his father to press his claim; Kashyapa warned him that Indra was the eldest of them all and foremost in accomplishments, strong by nature, devoted to the Brahmanas, grateful, the king of the whole world and the refuge of the good, holding his sovereignty because he worked for the well-being of all creatures — Vajranabha could not vanquish him and would be killed, as one who rouses a serpent meets his own destruction.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v1-6: 'After the termination of the sacrifice of Kashyapa... the gods and Asuras repaired to their respective habitations'; Vajranābha, 'desirous of conquering the three worlds, went to Kashyapa', who said: 'Sakra is the eldest of you all and the foremost in accomplishments: he is endued with great ascetic powers, is strong by nature, devoted to the Brāhmanas, grateful, the king of the whole world and the refuge of the good and the pious. Because he is engaged in the well-being of all creatures he has obtained this sovereignty... you will not be able to vanquish him but yourself will be killed. As one who excites the anger of a serpent meets with his own destruction, so you will in no time be destroyed'.

statements.claim: As a dying man lets pass the medicine that could save him, Vajranabha let the warning pass; he saluted his father and went home to gather kinsmen, warriors and friends, and his first march was against the celestial region itself.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v7-9: 'as a man, desirous of meeting with death... does not take medicine so Vajrānābha did not approve of the words of Kashyapa. Having saluted Kashyapa... he began to make arrangements for conquering the three worlds... collected his kinsmen, warriors, and friends. He first set out for conquering the region of the celestials'.

statements.claim: At that very time Indra and Krishna had sent their swans into the city of Vajra to bring about the Asura's ruin; hearing the swans' intelligence, the Yadava heroes consulted together: 'Vajranabha will be killed now, and by Pradyumna. But Vajranabha's daughter and Sunabha's two daughters are the devoted wives of our house, and all three are with child, near their time. What should we do?'
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v10-14: 'the highly powerful deities Indra and Upendra had sent the Swans there for bringing about Vajranābha's destruction'; the Yadus consulted: 'Forsooth Vajranābha will be killed now by Pradyumna. But Vajranābha's daughter and Sunābha's daughters are their devoted wives. They are all enciente and the time for their delivery is near at hand. What should we do now?' (Sunabha's two daughters, Chandravati and Gunavati, are identified in HV 1.241 v33-34.)

statements.claim: The two gods answered through the swans: 'Have no fear. Your sons will be beautiful as Kama and complete in every accomplishment; even in the womb they will master the Vedas with their auxiliaries. They will spring at once to youth, and they will be masters of every scripture.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v15-17: 'No fear: you will have beautiful sons like Kāma endued with all accomplishments; even when in the womb they will master all the Vedas with their auxilliaries. Your sons will at once grow to youth and they will be masters of all future topics and various scriptures'.

statements.claim: In time Prabhavati bore a son, omniscient and youthful as his father; a month later Chandravati bore Chandraprabha, the very image of Gada; and Gunavati bore Gunavan, beautiful and equally omniscient — the three boys grew swiftly, mastering every shastra, and played along the high turrets of the palaces, where the Daityas posted in the sky could see them and carried the news straight to Vajranabha, who was already preparing his war against heaven.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v19-24: 'Prabhāvati gave birth to a son, omniscient and youthful after his father. The son Chandraprabha, resembling Gada, whom Chandravati gave birth to after a month... Gunavati too gave birth to a similiarly beautiful son by name Gunavān'; the boys 'began to grow up... mastering all the Shastras. They used to move about on the turrets of the palaces and at the desire of Indra and Upendra they were seen (by the Daityas)... As soon as they saw them the Daityas, stationed in the sky, respectfully communicated it to Vajranābha who was desirous of conquering the celestial region'.

statements.claim: 'Arrest them,' said Vajranabha, 'those who have trespassed into my house'; at his order soldiers closed every quarter of the city and the cry went up on all sides — 'Arrest them — kill them'; the young mothers, who loved their sons, wept in fear, and Pradyumna steadied them: 'While we are alive and firm, you need not fear. The Daityas will not be able to touch us.'
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v25-29: Vajranābha: 'Arrest them who have trespassed into my house'; 'the soldiers guarded all the quarters... there arose on all sides exclamations, "Arrest them speedily kill them"'; 'the mothers, fond of sons, began to weep in fear. Pradyumna encouraged them, saying: "So long we are alive and firm you need not fear... The Daityas will not be able to do any thing to us"'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna laid the whole choice before Prabhavati: her father, uncles, brothers and all her kinsmen were waiting with clubs in their hands and for her sake deserved respect and honor, but the time was dreadful and the Danava kings meant to kill them — if they bore it they would die, if they fought they would succeed; he asked her to consult with her two sisters, saying they were under her orders.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v30-33: Pradyumna to Prabhāvati: 'your father, uncles, brothers kinsmen and other relatives are waiting with clubs in their hands. For you they deserve our respect and honor. But the time is very dreadful. The Dānava kings, desirous of killing us, will fight with us. If we bear it we shall have to die. If we fight we will meet with success. Consult with your two sisters and tell us what we should do for we are now under your orders'.

statements.claim: Prabhavati knelt, weeping, her hands on her forehead, and urged Pradyumna to take up his arms and protect himself, so that he would see his wife and sons; she bade him remember Rukmini and Aniruddha and save himself from the peril, trusting the boon of the great rishi, effulgent as sun and fire, that she would lead a blameless life, never be a widow, and that her sons would live.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v34-38: 'Placing her hands on her forehead and kneeling down Prabhāvati, weeping, said: "O descendant of Yadu... take up your arms and protect yourself. If you yourself survive you will see your wife and sons. Remember the honarable Vaidarbhi and Aniruddha and save yourself from this peril... the great and intelligent Rishi had conferred on me the boon that I would lead a blameless life for ever, would not be a widow and my sons would live... the words of the Rishi, effulgent like the sun and fire, will not be falsified"'. (Vaidarbhi = Rukmini, the princess of Vidarbha — the story's 'Rukmini' is the same person.)

statements.claim: She rose, rinsed her mouth, and took up a sword; the jewel of a woman placed it in Pradyumna's hands, saying 'Acquire victory'; bending low, Pradyumna bowed his head to the blade and accepted it with joy; and Chandravati, delightedly, gave a sword to Gada, and Gunavati gave another such weapon to the mighty Shamba.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt + HV 1.243 v39-41: Prabhāvati 'handed over a sword to Rukshmini's son... saying, "Acquire victory"'; full text: 'Bending low his head and bowing unto it the virtuous souled Pradyumna delightedly accepted the sword offered by his devoted wife. Chandravati delightedly gave to Gada one Nishtringsha and Gunavati gave another such weapon to the highly powerful Shāmva'.

notes: Faithful to HV 1.243 v1-41 (pack passage complete through v38; the sword-giving beat v39-41 is confirmed by the pack excerpt line and the same Gutenberg text). The pack and story are in exact agreement throughout, including the rishi's boon and the arming of Gada and Shamba by Sunabha's daughters.

statements.claim: While the cries of 'Arrest them, kill them' still rang through the city of Vajra, Pradyumna, by his power of illusion, created a celestial car and made Ananta, the thousand-headed serpent, foremost of his class, its charioteer.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt: 'Pradyumna... created a car with his Māyā. He made the thousand-headed Nāga Ananta... his charioteer'; HV 1.243 v42-44 (same Gutenberg text): Pradyumna 'created a car with his Māyā. He made the thousand-headed Nāga Ananta, the foremost of their class, his charioteer'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna told his kinsmen to hold the ground and fight the Danavas below while he took the battle to the sky, and the soldiers sent to seize the trespassers found a household already in arms.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v42-44: Pradyumna said to Hansaketu, 'remain here with Shāmva and fight with the Dānavas. I will fight in the sky, protecting all the quarters' — the story's 'his kinsmen' is a fair generalization (the source names one addressee), and the arrest order of the preceding verses (v25-27) is the 'trespassers' context.

statements.claim: Like fire running over dry grass, Pradyumna swept through the midst of the Asura army, gladdening Prabhavati as he rode; crescent-shaped arrows, dreadful as serpents — some sharp-headed, some blunt — streamed from his bow into the ranks of the sons of Diti; the Asuras, resolute and maddened with battle fury, struck back with every weapon, but he cut off arms decked with armlets and heads without number, until severed heads and bodies covered the earth; Indra and the gods watched the battle of Daityas and Yadavas with pleasure, and the Daityas who turned upon Gada and Shamba met their destruction like boats in a mighty ocean.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v45-51: 'As fire ranges on grass, so he, ascending that best of cars, and gladdening Prabhāvati, began to move about in the midst of the Asura army. With crescent-shaped arrows, dreadful like serpents, some with sharp heads and some blunt he began to assail the sons of Diti'; 'the Asuras too, resolute and maddened with battle fury... struck the lotus-eyed son of Kamala's lord. Krishna's son cut off the arms of some decked with Keyuras and the heads of many... filled the surface of the earth. The king of gods, the victor of armies, along with the gods, began to witness with pleasure the battle between the Daityas and Bhaimas. The Daityas, who ran after Gada and Sāmva, met with destruction like a boat in a mighty ocean'.

statements.claim: Sensing that the Asura king's ascetic merit had run out, spirits (Bhutas) entered the city wherever they pleased, and the Asuras who had lived well-fed and safe behind their king's boon found their walls meaning nothing.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v57: 'Thinking "His ascetic virtue is gone and this wicked one is to be killed by the Yadavas" the Bhutas entered wherever they liked'.

statements.claim: With the permission of Brahma, Krishna sent his own car to Gada, with Matali's son to drive it; Indra sent his elephant Airavata to Shamba, with the twice-born Pravara riding it; and the celestial youth Jayanta came to stand at Pradyumna's side — after which Pradyumna and Jayanta pressed through the very palaces of the city, destroying the Asuras with a net of arrows, so that no corner of Vajra was safe from them.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v52-58: 'Hari, the lord of gods... sent his own car to Gada and asked Mātali's son Suvarchhā to become its driver. The Lord Indra sent his Airāvata to Shāmva and engaged Pravara to ride it. He sent Jayanta as an assistant to Rukshmini's son'; '(with the permission of Brahmā... Sakra... had sent there the car driven by Mātali's son and the Airāvata with the celestial youth Jayanta and the best of the twice-born Pravara)'; 'Gradually entering into their palaces the highly powerful Pradyumna and Jayanta began to destroy the Asuras with a net-work of arrows'. NB the Dutt text itself credits the car to Hari in v52 and to Sakra in v55-56 and v59-60; the story mirrors both attributions, so neither is an error.

statements.claim: In the midst of the slaughter Pradyumna called to Gada that Indra had sent the car, that Matali's son was its driver and that the elephant ridden by Pravara was for Shamba; that there was a great worship of Rudra at Dwaraka that day, and when it ended Krishna himself would come the next day, and by his orders they would kill the sinful Vajranabha together with his kinsmen; and he warned that they must take care that Vajranabha did not kill them and their sons, for the destruction of one's own sons is worse than one's own death — they should protect their sons by every means.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v59-64: Pradyumna to Gada: 'the king of gods has sent for you this car with the horses. The highly powerful son of Mātali is its driver. This elephant Airāvata, ridden by Pravara, has been sent for Shāmva... there will be a great Pujā of Rudra at Dwārakā to-day. After its termination the highly powerful Hrishikesha will come here to-morrow. According to his orders we will kill this sinful Vajranābha together with his kinsmen... we should so carefully concert measures that he may not kill us with our sons. The destruction of one's own sons in this world is more than his death. Therefore the learned should protect their sons by all means'.

statements.claim: Pradyumna then multiplied himself by his illusory power into millions of forms and dispelled the darkness the Daityas had cast over the field; wherever an enemy turned there Krishna's son stood, so that creatures seemed to see him in every foe, and the king of gods was pleased to see the destroyer of enemies everywhere at once.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v65-67: Pradyumna 'made, by his illusory power, millions of his own self and dispelled the dreadful darkness created by the Daityas. Seeing him... the king of gods was highly pleased. As the Divine soul lives in all human souls so the creatures saw Krishna's son in every one of the enemies'.

statements.claim: All through the night the battle raged; when Jayanta went down to the Ganga that issues from Vishnu's foot for his evening prayers, Pradyumna fought the Daityas alone, and when Pradyumna in his turn recited his evening prayers in the celestial Ganga, Jayanta alone held the host — and when dawn came, three in every four of the Asuras lay dead.
statements.evidence: HV 1.243 v68-70: 'The highly powerful son of Rukshmini thus fighting the night elapsed and three fourths of the Asuras were killed'; 'when Jayanta repaired to the Ganges issuing from Vishnu's feet for reciting his evening prayers, Krishna's son fought alone with the Daityas. And afterwards when Pradyumna recited his evening prayers in the etherial Gangā the highly powerful Jayanta alone fought with the Daityas'; pack excerpt: 'three fourths of the Asuras were killed'.

statements.claim: At sunrise the field was still: the army that had marched out to conquer heaven lay broken around the city, and only its king remained — untouched, at the center of the ruin, waiting.
statements.evidence: Closing transition to the next episode: three-fourths of the Asuras slain and the night battle ended are supported (v68); that Vajranabha alone remained 'untouched' is cliffhanger emphasis — he is indeed still alive and duels Krishna's son at sunrise in ch. 244.

notes: The whole battle scene of HV 1.243 lies beyond the pack's visible passage (which cuts off mid-sentence at v38-39, '[...]'); every story beat was verified against the pack's excerpt line plus the same cited Gutenberg translation (chapter CCXLIII). The car-to-Gada attribution varies between Hari and Sakra within the Dutt text itself (v52 vs v55-56/59-60) — the story faithfully mirrors the source and its own dialogue is consistent. The pack index ('Indra sends his own car...') is a coarse paraphrase of the same dual-attribution passage.
